title: The pandits of Kashmir
hookLine: Kashmiri Brahmins facing forced conversion come to him for help

cards: Spring of 1675, at Anandpur. The Guru is home, and his young son, Gobind Rai, is with him. A group of travelers arrives from the far north, from the valley of Kashmir, worn out from the mountain roads.
They are pandits, Hindu Brahmin scholars and priests. They are not Sikhs. They've come a long way to ask a Guru for help.

teach.b: Here is what the pandits told the Guru, as Sikh tradition remembers it.
Under the emperor Aurangzeb, the Mughal governor of Kashmir was pressing Hindus there to convert to Islam, and the Brahmins, as religious leaders, were under particular pressure.

Tradition names their leader Pandit Kirpa Ram, from Mattan, near Anantnag. They had nowhere else to turn. Historians discuss how widespread this policy was, and how the court saw it; the sources are not all agreed.
What the Sikh sources agree on is the scene at Anandpur, and three things stand out.

teach.h: NOT HIS FOLLOWERS, NOT HIS THREAD.
teach.b: First, the pandits were not the Guru's followers. They wore the sacred thread and the forehead mark, practices the Gurus themselves had not taken up.
On day six you met Guru Nanak as a boy, refusing to wear it. Second, the Guru's own community was not being threatened in this request. He could have said: this isn't our fight.
Third, the Guru listened. Tradition says he sat quietly for a long time, deep in thought, heavy with what they had told him.
The question in the air was simple and terrible: who would stand up for the right of other people to practice a faith that wasn't his? His answer, and what it cost, come in the days ahead.

Look back at this week: a word changed to please a court; a child Guru, calm before the powerful, who served the sick and died in Delhi; a boy renamed brave of the sword, who went quiet at Bakala; a trader shouting from a roof; a new town on rough ground.
And now this: the people in need came to him, and he did not send them away.

how: Sikhs tell the story of the Kashmiri pandits coming to Anandpur as the beginning of Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom, and honor him as one who gave his life for the freedom of others to practice their faith.

games.q: you're the Guru. people of another faith, not your followers, come asking for help against forced conversion. what do you do?
o: tell them it isn't your community's fight.
sit with them, and take their plea to heart.
games.why: tradition says the Guru sat long in thought, heavy with their story. what he decided comes in the next days.

practice: Think of someone who came to you lately, even in a small way: a message you skimmed, a friend who said I'm fine too quickly, a coworker who needed more than they asked for.
Replay it slowly, and this time just listen, without planning your answer, noticing what they were really asking. Stay with them, the way the Guru sat with the travelers.

wordCard.voice: Kirpa Ram. The Brahmin leader of the Kashmiri pandits who traveled to Anandpur in 1675 to ask Guru Tegh Bahadur for help.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: Kashmiri pandits, Brahmin scholars of the Kashmir valley.

carryVoice: Your line: they came to him. A knock at the door, and a long silence while he listened. Day seventy-seven, the end of another week.
